title: Why lost people walk in circles

qwen.narrator: A warm, confident American male narrator in his thirties with a friendly, slightly amused storytelling tone. Clear diction, brisk and lively pace, expressive like a popular YouTube explainer telling a funny true story.
qwen.hiker: A cheerful, slightly goofy middle-aged German man speaking English with a light German accent. Overconfident and enthusiastic, a bit loud.

qwen_candidates.A_deep: A deep, rich American male voice with a dramatic, cinematic storytelling style, confident and punchy, medium-fast pace.
qwen_candidates.B_playful: A playful, high-energy young American male narrator, fast-paced and expressive with comic timing, like a viral short-video storyteller.
qwen_candidates.C_british: A dry, witty British male narrator in his forties, calm but amused, crisp diction, like a clever documentary host.

lines.text: Get lost in a forest, and your own legs will secretly walk you in a giant circle.
Meet Klaus. He's lost in a German forest.

lines.speaker: hiker
lines.text: Easy. I'll just walk in a straight line.
An hour later, he finds a campfire.
Nobody's there, so he marches on. Dead straight. Another hour. Another campfire. Same log. Same sad sausage.
In 2009, scientists tested this. They sent people into a German forest with GPS trackers and told them to walk straight.
When the sun was out, they managed it. Under clouds, they looped back over their own path, without noticing.
Blindfolded in an open field, some walked circles just twenty metres wide.
And it isn't one leg being longer. With nothing to steer by, tiny errors in your sense of straight pile up, and curl you round.
So if you're ever lost, aim at a landmark far ahead, walk to it, then pick another.

experiment.hypothesis: Ricks Clips structure: a comic escalating story with the science reveal later, a cut every ~2 s across several small sets, face close-ups, near-continuous narration.
facts: Souman, Frissen, Sreenivasa & Ernst, 'Walking straight into circles', Current Biology 19:1538 (2009): GPS-tracked walkers in the Bienwald forest (Germany) and the Sahara walked in circles when the sun was hidden, repeatedly crossing their own path without noticing; with the sun or moon visible they kept fairly straight; blindfolded walkers made circles as small as 20 m across. https://www.mpg.de/596269/pressrelease200908171
